photos.label: Dense upright blue-green leafy bunch of Lindheimer muhly — mature flowering panicle and exposed ligule not shown
photos.creator: Cody Stricker

field_rule: First check SCALE and the BASAL BUNCH: Lindheimer muhly forms a large coarse, densely tufted fountain often around 0.8–1.5 m tall, with tall relatively contracted, densely flowered panicles. At the leaf collar a LONG MEMBRANOUS ligule is the high-value confirmation; photograph it with a ruler rather than inferring it from plant size.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Kew GrassBase contracted 20–40 cm panicle; UT Austin Williamson County M. lindheimeri aging more open/feathery 30–62.5 cm panicle
head.reference: Young contracted head may appear long_narrow_panicle, older opened/loosely feathery head may appear airy; photo-first both allowed. This is variation within species and different descriptions, NOT proof of hybrid.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the TRUE long membrane at the leaf collar
diagnostic_checks.check: A firm, eciliate MEMBRANOUS ligule is usually 8–15 mm in the Kew treatment. Its pale triangular sheath base must be opened at the actual blade–sheath junction. A large fountain-shaped bunch alone is not species ID.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Seep muhly generally has a shorter 2–4(9) mm membrane and much narrower 1–2 mm threadlike rolled blades; the hybrid overlaps both parents.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; collar scale photo on authenticated local plant pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Muhlenbergia lindheimeri

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare YOUNG contracted and OLDER opening panicles
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes a narrow, densely flowered panicle ~20–40 cm by 1–1.5 cm; a Williamson County Texas specimen account describes an older, more open/feathery 30–62.5 cm panicle. Stage, branch width and treatment vary. Record actual stage; do NOT reject mature spreading heads as impossible.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Seep muhly is a much more open 10–30 cm wide-oval cloud; Canyon hybrid falls between and requires floret anatomy.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Cross-source width/age differences retained; broad head candidate allows narrow and airy views without identifying hybrid from silhouette
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Muhlenbergia lindheimeri; UT Texas local account

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure glumes, floret and short awn on the SAME spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: A mature spikelet has ONE fertile floret, usually ~2–3.5 mm; paired glumes are each generally ~2–3.5 mm, roughly floret length, one-veined. Lemma three-veined, may be awnless or carry a fine 0–4 mm awn. Record a whole attached mature spikelet and mm ruler.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Seep muhly glumes tend to be much shorter (1–2.5 mm versus 3.5–5 mm spikelet). Canyon hybrid glumes ~2–2.5 and spikelet ~3–4 mm: strong overlap.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase plus Texas local specimen; overlapping sizes cannot alone certify a hybrid or parent
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Muhlenbergia lindheimeri

diagnostic_checks.look: Confirm the unusually long membranous ligule on an intact Lindheimer leaf
diagnostic_checks.check: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015, p. 54) describe a stiff membrane about 8–15 mm, acute and lacerate, and 2–3(5)-mm blades folded lengthwise, with the lower sheath often compressed and keeled. Seep muhly has finer arcuate/inrolled blades and a 2–9-mm membrane; ranges overlap. Compare the basal clump and mature panicle as well.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Muhlenbergia reverchonii (seep muhly), whose finer rolled leaves and smaller tuft should be checked together
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Direct 2015 regional vegetative reference; confirms existing membrane scoring but does NOT independently certify existing collar photo
diagnostic_checks.source: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015, p. 54

ligule.source: Kew GrassBase Panicum virgatum + FNA/UMass field descriptions
ligule.reference: True ligule is a ciliate MEMBRANE; after it abrades it may LOOK like dense white hair fringe. Hair triangle on upper blade is a SEPARATE structure. Both visual collar options permitted to avoid false exclusion.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the hair TRIANGLE and true ligule separately
diagnostic_checks.check: Switchgrass commonly shows a wedge/triangle of hairs on the UPPER blade surface immediately above the collar. Its anatomical ligule is a CILIATE MEMBRANE; some descriptions note it wears away leaving a prominent ring of white hairs. The hair patch is NOT the ligule.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Indiangrass has the conspicuous rifle-sight pointed auricles on either side of a membranous ligule; Hall's panicgrass lacks the robust switchgrass collar and rhizome combination.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew/FNA/UMass sources; same-plant opened collar photo pending, two broad visual appearances accepted
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Panicum virgatum; field collar description

diagnostic_checks.look: Expose the long, scaly rhizomes under a mature flowering culm
diagnostic_checks.check: Large perennial switchgrass usually has sturdy scaly creeping RHIZOMES connecting shoots; FNA descriptions note variable tufted and sod-forming ecotypes. Its large airy, typically 15–55 cm long panicle can persist dry into winter.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Kleingrass may have very short knotty rhizomes but not the same long stout scaly system; witchgrass is an annual with a loose fall tumblehead.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and Kew; no winter rooted same-plant photo certified; don't infer rhizomes from a detached clump
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum virgatum

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare the wide, large two-floret spikelets with Hall's and kleingrass
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA allows broad intraspecific spikelet variation (~2.5–8 mm); Kew typical GrassBase 3–5 mm. The lower glume is roughly 1/2–4/5 length, with prominent veins; upper glume and lower staminate lemma exceed the smooth, shiny smaller fertile upper floret. Don't interpret separate florets as separate spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hall's panicgrass has mainly 2.2–3.9 mm spikelets in close clusters; kleingrass mainly 2.5–3.5 mm spikelets with a lower glume often only 1/3 length.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Species-wide source measurement range differs; no universal spikelet cutoff or exact local specimen proof
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum virgatum

field_rule: Knotgrass combines wet-ground creeping stolons with usually paired (rarely three) unilateral flowering racemes. Bahia grass can produce two racemes but differs in low turf/rhizome architecture and spikelet structure. Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Flora of North America, Paspalum distichum
head.reference: Usually two near-digitate branches, sometimes a third below; allow paired_spikes and general one_sided in broad visual selection until detailed head photo QA.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 230
habit.reference: Long trailing culms rooting at nodes in wet areas; mat-forming appearance may be observed.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the flowering branch all the way to its base
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually TWO terminal, spreading, one-sided branches arise very close together; FNA also allows a THIRD below the pair. Mature branches are approximately 1.4–7 cm; do not exclude a plant with three branches.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Thin paspalum can have one to several branches but also axillary flowering heads; tall Dallisgrass usually has more separate branches.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Flora of North America species description; attachment photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: FNA — Paspalum distichum

diagnostic_checks.look: Check if the spikelets are solitary or paired
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes mostly SINGLE 2.4–3.2 mm spikelets along each flat, winged branch axis (rarely paired). The LOWER glume is absent or a tiny triangular scale; the upper glume and lower sterile lemma each have three veins.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Most of the other six Paspalum species here have paired spikelets; Urochloa has a more developed lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; magnified attached branch needed
diagnostic_checks.source: FNA — Paspalum distichum

diagnostic_checks.look: Document an actual surface runner and rooting node
diagnostic_checks.check: Look for long creeping stolons or rhizomes in wet ground and a node that roots into the soil. A rooted runner with leaves is a stem, not an ordinary fibrous root. Compare the living crown along the bank.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass and Vaseygrass mainly form erect clumps with only very short knotty rhizomes, not long mats.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA account plus regional field observations; connected photo needed
diagnostic_checks.source: FNA — Paspalum distichum

field_rule: Actual archived Bob Harms whole flowering-specimen panel 1 shows several attached leafy shoots and panicles; panel 2 displays the entire dense short-branched seedhead; panel 3 magnifies overlapping glumes. A contracted ovoid to cylindrical head is a first clue (FNA 0.5–8 cm long, often 0.8–2 cm wide), but several introduced Phalaris look similar. The one- vs two-STERILE-LEMMA difference cannot be determined from head silhouette alone.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 234
head.reference: Compact, narrow cylindrical SPICELIKE PANICLE, not a true simple grass spike.

ligule.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 234

fertile_sterile_florets.source: UT Austin PRC Williamson County Phalaris caroliniana; Kew GrassBase
fertile_sterile_florets.reference: 3 florets per spikelet: TWO basal sterile (small/awl-shaped lemmas) + ONE upper bisexual fertile floret; narrow winged glume keels. The broad photos cannot independently certify this without dissection.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the DENSE head: it is a PANICLE, not a true spike
diagnostic_checks.check: Carolina canarygrass is an ANNUAL with a compact ovate to cylindrical spike-like panicle usually ~1–7 cm long, 0.8–2 cm wide. Short densely branched rays carry spikelets; a short head alone cannot distinguish it from other canarygrasses.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Annual beardgrass also has dense heads but their fuzzy outline comes from long AWNS on the glumes; Phalaris is typically unawned.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and UT Williamson County, existing head photo helps silhouette only
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Phalaris caroliniana

diagnostic_checks.look: Count TWO small basal STERILE florets beneath one fertile floret
diagnostic_checks.check: A Phalaris caroliniana spikelet has THREE florets TOTAL: the two lower ones sterile and represented by thin, small, hairy 1.2–2.5 mm lemmas; the upper fertile floret has a much larger smooth-to-hairy cartilaginous 3–4.7 mm lemma. Count florets by dissection.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other Phalaris species such as P. minor may have only ONE developed basal sterile lemma; do not identify all Phalaris from compact panicle alone.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew and UT Texas species account both explicitly give 2 sterile + 1 bisexual; specific plant dissection pending
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin — Phalaris caroliniana

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the WINGED glume keels and true membrane ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Strongly flattened ~4.2–5.6 mm glumes have three or sometimes five veins, with a NARROW translucent WING on each keel above midpoint. The inner true ligule is a visible 1–6.5 mm membrane in a Texas specimen account.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Polypogon glumes have a split/notched tip and long projecting awns that create fuzz; canarygrass lacks that glume-awn halo.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew / UT local specimen measurements; close detached glume and inner collar image pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Phalaris caroliniana

sexual_system.source: Flora of North America Poa annua
sexual_system.reference: Usually annual, not rhizomatous; gynomonoecious reproductive system, not separate dioecious male/female plants as P. arachnifera.

diagnostic_checks.look: Observe the short flowering stem AND its rooted crown
diagnostic_checks.check: Annual bluegrass is normally an annual (rarely persists another season), densely tufted and without true rhizomes; culms in FNA usually 2–20 cm and the panicle only 1–7(10) cm. A low plant alone is not diagnostic.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas bluegrass is taller, perennial and rhizomatous; heavily mown plants of either can mislead
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; rooted specimen and cut-age variation pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Poa annua

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure one intact spikelet and leaf ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Typical spikelets are 3–5 mm with 2–6 florets; lemmas 2.5–4 mm. The TRUE ligule is a smooth membrane, normally 0.5–3 mm (up to 5), despite a hooded leaf tip; the tip is shared by other Poa.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas bluegrass often has larger, dense spikelet arrays and sex-specific floret features
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; attached floral parts need macro
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Poa annua

diagnostic_checks.look: Do not mistake one sex for separate male/female plants
diagnostic_checks.check: Poa annua can bear female and perfect florets in its sexual system; it is not the strictly dioecious Texas bluegrass. Inspect reproductive structures, not just the green/blue color of leaves.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Poa arachnifera has male and female flowers on separate plants
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA reproductive source; requires flowering plants
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Poa annua

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon, Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, 1999 (user-provided monocots excerpt)

sexual_system.source: Flora of North America Poa arachnifera
sexual_system.reference: Strictly dioecious; pistillate florets with 3 long silky callus webs (4–10 mm), staminate flowers may lack conspicuous webs. Do not require female webs on every plant.

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate a real underground rhizome
diagnostic_checks.check: Texas bluegrass is a perennial with slender spreading rhizomes. FNA describes culms 20–85 cm and mostly narrow crowded flowering heads 3–12(18) cm; winter-green shoots are not proof alone.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Annual bluegrass lacks rhizomes, is usually much shorter, and may open its panicle with age
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; exact rhizome connection/photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Poa arachnifera

diagnostic_checks.look: Identify the sex before inspecting cobweb hairs
diagnostic_checks.check: The species is strictly dioecious: an entire plant has functionally pistillate OR staminate florets. FEMALE floret calluses have three conspicuous silky webs of hairs about 4–10 mm. Male florets may have little or no webbing; lack of webbing on a male is not absence of this species.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Poa annua has different reproductive biology, without the female-specific 3-web Texas bluegrass pattern
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA female/male anatomy checked; both sex samples still need photographs
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Poa arachnifera

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the female lemma and true ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives pistillate lemmas about 4.2–6.4 mm, and a true membrane ligule 1–4 mm; do not mistake cobwebby hairs at the floret's callus for the ligule at the leaf collar.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Poa annua has much smaller panicles and lemmas and a similarly membranous ligule
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA checked; needs paired macro at same scale
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Poa arachnifera

habit.reference: Sorghum bicolor is annual and lacks the perennial rhizome system of Johnsongrass.

awns.reference: Subsp. bicolor usually awnless; subsp. drummondii fertile lemmas awned about 10 mm. Do not use fixed awn choice for the species complex.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect annual growth and mature grain exposure
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes an annual or occasionally short-lived plant without rhizomes; cultivated grain types often have large visible caryopses between spreading glumes at maturity. Weedy Sudan/shattercane forms may behave differently.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Johnsongrass maintains long creeping rhizomes and its grain is not typically exposed
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; cultivar and life-stage variation flagged
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Sorghum bicolor

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the sessile/pedicelled pair and disarticulation
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives a 3–9 mm bisexual sessile spikelet and smaller 3–6 mm pedicelled sterile or male companion; inflorescences range from loose to extremely compact. Cultivated rames often remain intact; shattercane-like forms may fragment.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Johnsongrass is regularly rhizomatous and has smaller often readily disarticulating rames
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; cultivated and weedy taxon variability
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Sorghum bicolor

diagnostic_checks.look: Record the awn but never require one fixed length

diagnostic_checks.compare: Johnsongrass has variably awned paired units, so confirm intact roots and mature fruit structure
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; selected variety/subspecies uncertain
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Sorghum bicolor

photos.creator: Cody Stricker

field_rule: Use visible macro morphology first and defer difficult perennial-species separations to mature material, reliable grain tests and microscope when necessary.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses
broad_group_note: Existing Hays Botany description screened; historical flora treats Sporobolus compositus in infraspecific aggregates that do not directly map to all modern accepted species. Retain provisional head/habit states and flag taxon crosswalk.

head.reference: Vertical narrow panicle often partly enclosed by subtending upper sheath; contracted spike-like appearance, not a true single spike.

ligule.reference: Tiny CILIATE MEMBRANOUS ligule; hair fringe and membrane both permitted as broad photographic appearances. Taxon complexes/varieties still unresolved.

pericarp.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center, Bob Harms, Texas Sporobolus complexes
pericarp.reference: Many modern keys use gelatinizing/swelling pericarp when wet vs non-gelatinizing in S. clandestinus. UT explains ambiguity of wet/moist/loose terms; requires multiple grains and lemma pubescence, not binary photograph based choice.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look for the partly SHEATHED tall contracted panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Tall/composite dropseed is usually a tufted perennial with narrow contracted flowering panicles ~5–26 cm, often partly hidden by the subtending leaf sheath. The ligule is a very short ciliate membrane/hair-fringe at field scale.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Poverty dropseed is an annual with much shorter 1–4 cm terminal AND axillary often sheathed panicles; S. clandestinus also forms narrow enclosed perennial heads.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Iowa grass account and UT Texas complex; sheath photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Iowa State — Sporobolus compositus

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine LEMMA surface rather than assuming all rough dropseed names agree
diagnostic_checks.check: The S. compositus complex is often diagnosed by relatively smooth, GLABROUS mature fertile lemma vs the visibly pubescent/scabrous opaque lemma of S. clandestinus. Typical S. compositus 4.5–5.4 mm single-floret spikelets and lemmas ~4.4–5.2 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: S. clandestinus typical 5–7 mm spikelets with pubescent 4–5 mm lemmas. Variation and both current/older names exist; compare actual same-scale spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Iowa State and UT Bob Harms; species-complex and variety interpretations not interchangeable
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center — Sporobolus compositus complex

diagnostic_checks.look: Be cautious with the moist pericarp test
diagnostic_checks.check: Pericarp of S. compositus is generally reported swelling/gelatinizing on soaking, whereas S. clandestinus stays loose but not gelatinous. UT Harms documents disagreement and ambiguity about interpreting 'loose', 'moist', and 'wet': a single uncertain drop does not confirm an identification.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Never perform a destructive wet seed test on the only voucher; record several grains and microscope lemma surface first.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: UT Texas detailed critique of pericarp key vs FNA/Riggins; source-qualified evidence, not pass/fail filter
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Plant Resources Center — Sporobolus pericarp caveats

diagnostic_checks.look: Separate the male upper section from female lower section

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the female rachis joint and inner collar

field_rule: Rank photos by what they truly show: flowering branch/shape first, followed by mature spikelet length and lower glume measured under 10–20×. Do not treat unmeasured photogenic heads as proof of native versus introduced species.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 259
head.reference: Compact panicle of erect-appressed one-sided spikelet-bearing branches.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 259
habit.reference: Annual that may creep and root from lower nodes; not always an upright tuft.

ligule.source: Kew GrassBase under Brachiaria texana; UT Austin regional morphology
ligule.reference: True ligule is a ciliate MEMBRANE, ~1–1.5 mm (UT Austin 1–1.8 mm). Hairlike cilia conceal the membrane base; retain hair and membrane broad visual states, not absence.

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the true collar beneath the hair fringe
diagnostic_checks.check: Texas signalgrass has a ciliate MEMBRANE 1–1.5 mm, often appearing like pure hairs until magnified. Regional UT Austin material describes a 1–1.8 mm fused membrane at the blade–sheath joint.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum usually has a more evident plain papery ligule; collar shape alone is genus-level.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase / UT Texas morphology; retain both broad visual states pending actual photo
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana under Brachiaria

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure spikelet and LOWER glume
diagnostic_checks.check: Published spikelets around 5–6 mm, paired along unilateral erect-appressed branches. The developed lower glume is around TWO-THIRDS the spikelet, usually 5–7 veined. The upper glume is about full spikelet length.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum mostly has no lower glume; Brownseed signalgrass has smaller 2.4–3 mm spikelets and a much shorter lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew source checked; mature same-plant dissection needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana

diagnostic_checks.look: Look at the textured upper fertile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: The hard upper fertile lemma is usually 3.5–4 mm, finely wrinkled across its back. Plants may be upright or sprawl and root at low nodes. Verify the annual growth base as well as a complete head.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other Urochloa species also have wrinkled fertile lemmas: combine with the large spikelet and lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase checked; local specimen and photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.
